title: Cockatoos and parrots

identification.basis: The dictionary names the black cockatoo in both dialects, the lorikeet, the king parrot and the fig parrot. Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas records the rainbow lorikeet, pale-headed rosella, galah, red-winged parrot, red-tailed black cockatoo, sulphur-crested cockatoo, scaly-breasted lorikeet and cockatiel.

summary: **[kadanji](word:kadanji)** in Yalanji and **[kumurbina](word:kumurbina)** in Nyungkul is the black cockatoo, the red-tailed black cockatoo that cracks the [bloodwood](entry:bloodwood) fruit in flocks of hundreds and screams across the river at evening; **[birrbirr](word:birrbirr)** is the rainbow lorikeet and any parrot; **[karrambil](word:karrambil)** the 'king parrot', which here is the red-winged parrot; **[yinjul](word:yinjul)** the fig parrot; and **[mirrimbal](word:mirrimbal)** the cockatoo's crest and the hat made of its feathers [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-rtbc]. The rainbow lorikeet is the most-recorded bird within 30 km of [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters), sixty-seven records, with the pale-headed rosella at fifty-two, the galah at thirty-six, the red-winged parrot at thirty-four, the red-tailed black cockatoo at thirty and the sulphur-crested cockatoo at eighteen [ref:ala-aves]. All of them live in hollows and on seed and blossom, which makes them the birds of the old trees: 'seed eaters and cavity nesters, and as such depend on trees with fairly large diameters' [ref:wiki-rtbc]. Roth's cockatoo hunters swam out under a head of grass to the drinking log and pulled the birds under, threw light boomerangs into the flocks, climbed to the roost by a lawyer cane at night with a stick, or limed the branches with fig-sap [ref:roth1901]. The feathers went into the camp's ornaments and the children's games, and the cockatoo's crest into the men's hat [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[kadanji](word:kadanji)** 'black cockatoo (Yalanji)' and **[kumurbina](word:kumurbina)** 'black cockatoo (Nyungkul)'. **[birrbirr](word:birrbirr)** 'parrot, parakeet, lorikeet; rainbow lorikeet (parakeet)'. **[karrambil](word:karrambil)** 'king parrot'; the Australian king parrot of the east coast does not reach the Mitchell, and the red-winged parrot, red and green and recorded thirty-four times here, is the king parrot of the inland [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-red-winged-parrot] [ref:ala-aves]. **[yinjul](word:yinjul)** 'fig parrot', the tiny green parrot of the rainforest figs. **[mirrimbal](word:mirrimbal)** 'cockatoo crest; the name of a hat made from cockatoo feathers' [ref:hershberger1982]. In English the galah's name 'is derived from *gilaa*, a word from the Yuwaalaraay and neighbouring Aboriginal languages spoken in north-western New South Wales' [ref:wiki-galah].

sections.heading: The cockatoos and parrots of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
**Red-tailed black cockatoo** (*Calyptorhynchus banksii*, *kadanji*), thirty records. 'A large black cockatoo native to Australia. Adult males have a characteristic pair of bright red panels on the tail that gives the species its name.' 'Around 60 centimetres in length ... The male's plumage is all black with a prominent black crest made up of elongated feathers from the forehead and crown. The bill is dark grey. The tail is also black with two lateral bright red panels. Females are black with yellow-orange stripes in the tail and chest'. 'The species is usually found in eucalyptus woodlands, or along water courses. In the more northerly parts of the country, these cockatoos are commonly seen in large flocks. They are seed eaters and cavity nesters, and as such depend on trees with fairly large diameters, generally *Eucalyptus*' [ref:wiki-rtbc]. The split bloodwood fruit under a tree is its work; see [bloodwood](entry:bloodwood).

**Sulphur-crested cockatoo** (*Cacatua galerita*), eighteen records. 'A relatively large white cockatoo', '44–55 cm long ... Their plumage is overall white, while the underwing and tail are tinged yellow', with the yellow crest; 'distinctive, raucous calls can be very loud'; 'naturally curious, as well as very intelligent'; photographed 'feeding on *Pandanus* fruit' in the Territory [ref:wiki-scc].

**Galah** (*Eolophus roseicapilla*), thirty-six records. 'About 35 cm in length, and weighs 270–350 g. It has a pale silver to grey back, a pale grey rump, a pink face and breast, and a light pink mobile crest'; 'often found in flocks of 10 to 1,000 individuals', sometimes mixed with corellas and sulphur-crested cockatoos [ref:wiki-galah]. The **cockatiel** (*Nymphicus hollandicus*), three records, is the smallest cockatoo, 'found largely in arid or semi-arid country but always close to water. Largely nomadic, the species will move to where food and water is available' [ref:wiki-cockatiel].

**Rainbow lorikeet** (*Trichoglossus moluccanus*, *birrbirr*), sixty-seven records, the commonest bird in the list. 'A medium-sized parrot, with the length ranging from 25 to 30 cm, including the tail, and the weight varies from 75 to 157 g ... The head is deep blue with a greenish-yellow nuchal collar'; it feeds on nectar, pollen and fruit with a brush-tipped tongue, in screaming flocks at the blossom [ref:wiki-lorikeet]. The scaly-breasted lorikeet, four records, is its green cousin [ref:ala-aves].

**Pale-headed rosella** (*Platycercus adscitus*), fifty-two records. 'A moderate-size parrot with a pale yellow head, predominantly white cheeks, scalloped black and gold back and pale blue underparts'; 'found in open woodland, it feeds on seeds and fruit. As with other rosellas, the pale-headed rosella nests in hollows of large trees'; '33 cm long, which includes the 15 cm length of its tail'; the northern form 'is found from the Cape York Peninsula south through to Cardwell' [ref:wiki-rosella].

**Red-winged parrot** (*Aprosmictus erythropterus*, *karrambil*), thirty-four records. 'Typically about 30 to 33 cm in length. Both sexes have bright red wings and a bright green body. The male birds have a black nape, lower blue back and rump'. 'A hollow space in a tree at a height of 11 m from the ground usually acts as nest'; 'their diet typical consists of seeds from eucalyptus, acacia, berries, flowers, and insects. The birds' call are ching-ching, chink-chink or thin screeching' [ref:wiki-red-winged-parrot].

**Roth's cockatoo hunting, 1901.** 'Corellas, galahs, and white cockatoos are entrapped on the water in the late afternoon in the upper Georgina River District. The hunter, after tying numerous grass twigs and leafy boughs round his head, neck, and face, which are thus completely concealed, will swim out to some log or snag projecting just out of the water, on which he has learnt, from previous observation, these birds have been accustomed to alight: here he supports himself, with only his head above the surface. As the birds come down to drink, they fly around the bushes, and resting on the log, etc., are easily caught by the legs, pulled under the water, their necks wrung, and stuck one after another in the hunter's waist-belt. Another and very common method throughout the North-West Central Districts of catching these and other birds which fly in mobs is to throw a light boomerang into their very midst when on the wing. On the lower Tully River the capture of the white cockatoo is somewhat of a difficult undertaking, but is mastered as follows: Having noticed the particular branch and tree on which these birds are wont to camp, the native will, during the daytime, climb the tree and fix a lawyer-cane to the branch in question: the cane is of such length that it reaches to the ground. At night-time he will climb it hand-over-hand fashion, fixing his feet as he progresses by grasping with the big and second toes; at the same time he carries with him a long, thin stick hanging down behind and attached to a ring of lawyer-cane round his forehead or neck. Having reached the branch singled out, he very stealthily crawls along it, and, sneaking up very carefully, knocks the birds over with the stick. This method of capture is somewhat of a hazardous one for the hunter, but is commonly and successfully employed.' The lower Tully people also used a bird-lime, *chimbun*, from the sap of a fig, 'for catching smaller birds, peewits, small parrots, and even young cockatoos ... spread not only along the branches where they roost, but also in and among the young blossoms' [ref:roth1901].

**Feathers.** At Bloomfield the children's spear-target wheel was 'decorated with parrot, pigeon or cockatoo feathers', and senior men wore a head ornament of 'cockatoo top-knot feathers stuck into beeswax', the dictionary's *mirrimbal* [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Telling them
sections.body:
- **Red-tailed black cockatoo**: all black, a slow heavy flight, red tail panels on the male, barred orange on the female; a wailing creak [ref:wiki-rtbc].
- **Sulphur-crested cockatoo**: white, yellow crest, screaming [ref:wiki-scc].
- **Galah**: pink and grey, in tumbling flocks [ref:wiki-galah].
- **Cockatiel**: small, grey, a yellow face and a long tail, in pairs near water [ref:wiki-cockatiel].
- **Rainbow lorikeet**: blue head, orange breast, green back, a fast screeching flight; the scaly-breasted lorikeet green with yellow scales [ref:wiki-lorikeet].
- **Pale-headed rosella**: yellow head, blue belly, scalloped back, a whistle [ref:wiki-rosella].
- **Red-winged parrot**: green with red shoulders, a slow deep flight, 'ching-ching' [ref:wiki-red-winged-parrot].
- **Fig parrot** (*yinjul*): tiny, green, in the rainforest figs to the east [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Split bloodwood and gum fruit** under a tree: black cockatoos [ref:wiki-rtbc].
- **A tree in blossom roaring with lorikeets** by day [ref:wiki-lorikeet].
- **Chewed hollow entrances** and a bird's head looking out in the breeding season [ref:wiki-rosella].
- **Galahs on the ground** at a dam, and cockatoos on the pandanus fruit by the river [ref:wiki-galah] [ref:wiki-scc].
- **A drinking log** where the birds come down in the late afternoon: Roth's ambush [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Where they live
sections.body: The hollow-bearing [woodland](entry:woodland), the river's gums and paperbarks, the pandanus and the figs; the black cockatoo 'in eucalyptus woodlands, or along water courses', the rosella 'in open woodland', the cockatiel and the galah on the open flats and at the dams [ref:wiki-rtbc] [ref:wiki-rosella] [ref:wiki-cockatiel] [ref:re-woodland]. Every one of them nests in a hollow, which only an old tree has.

sections.heading: The seed and blossom birds
sections.body: The cockatoos and parrots are what the woodland's seed and blossom turn into: the black cockatoo's year is the [bloodwood's](entry:bloodwood) crop, the lorikeet's the gum blossom's, the rosella's and galah's the grass seed on the ground [ref:wiki-rtbc] [ref:wiki-lorikeet] [ref:wiki-rosella]. They share the blossom with the [native bees](entry:native-bees), the honeyeaters and, at night, the [flying foxes](entry:woodland), and the hollows with the [possums](entry:possums), the ducks and the kookaburras [ref:wiki-rtbc]. The [brown goshawk](entry:eagles-and-hawks) 'often hunt[s] near farmland or wetlands, where birds such as ducks, cockatoos and pigeons' gather; the [carpet python](entry:pythons) takes them in the hollow [ref:wiki-brown-goshawk] [ref:wiki-carpet-python].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Flocks gather wherever a crop is heavy; the black cockatoos on the bloodwoods in the late dry, the lorikeets on whichever gum is flowering; nesting in the hollows with the build-up and the wet; the galahs and cockatiels on the dry flats and dams when the inland dries [ref:wiki-rtbc] [ref:wiki-cockatiel]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Meat**: the big birds, taken at the drinking log, with a boomerang, or at the roost [ref:roth1901].
- **Feathers**: the cockatoo's crest in beeswax for the men's hat, parrot and cockatoo feathers on the children's target wheel [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Finding the blossom and the fruit**: the lorikeets' noise and the cockatoos' split fruit [ref:wiki-lorikeet] [ref:wiki-rtbc].

sections.heading: Taking cockatoos the old way
sections.body:
From Roth [ref:roth1901]:

1. **Find the drinking log** the birds use in the late afternoon.
2. **Tie grass and leafy boughs round the head and face**, swim out and hold the log with only the head above water; as the birds settle, catch them by the legs and pull them under [ref:roth1901].
3. **Or a light boomerang** thrown into the flock on the wing [ref:roth1901].
4. **Or the night climb**: fix a lawyer cane from the roost branch to the ground by day, climb it hand over hand at night with a long stick hung from a cane ring round the neck, crawl along the branch and knock the birds down; 'somewhat of a hazardous one for the hunter' [ref:roth1901].
5. **Or bird-lime** on the roost branches and in the blossom [ref:roth1901].
6. **Keep the crest feathers** and the red tail panels; see [native bees](entry:native-bees) for the beeswax [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].
- A cockatoo's bill takes a finger off; handle by the legs as Roth's hunters did [ref:roth1901].
- The night climb is Roth's 'hazardous' method and belongs to people who climbed lawyer canes barefoot [ref:roth1901].
- A hollow tree with birds in it is worth more standing than for the one bird in it [ref:wiki-rtbc].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The lorikeets, rosellas, galahs and black cockatoos are the loud life of the Karma Waters river camps, and the black cockatoos' evening flight along the river is the station's clock [ref:ala-aves]. The dictionary's names are the coast's; the Western Yalanji words for the galah, the rosella and the cockatiel are for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].
